title: "Risk and controls vocabulary"
order: 5

## The ticket

Wednesday afternoon at Lakeshore Blood Center, two deviations land on your Quality Analyst's
desk within four hours of each other.

**Deviation A:** a donor's required callback — a follow-up question on a travel-history item
from the eligibility interview — went out a day late. The unit stayed quarantined the entire
time; nothing shipped; the donor answered the question fine once reached. No product was ever
at risk.

**Deviation B:** a platelet unit had its label swapped with a physically adjacent unit during
component processing — correct blood type, wrong donor ID printed on the bag. It was caught at
the final pre-release barcode scan, seconds before it would have loaded onto the hospital
courier van. It did not leave the building.

Your Quality Analyst ranks the label mix-up "high" and the late callback "low," and wants to
open a CAPA (corrective and preventive action) for the label issue only, closing the callback
deviation with a note. Before it goes into this month's quality council packet, she asks you to
concur.

You don't have a gut check for this yet. Both events ended with zero patient impact. Both were
"caught." So what actually makes one deviation more dangerous than the other, and why does
"caught in time" not automatically mean "handled"? That's the vocabulary this lesson gives you.

## Why this vocabulary exists

You already do this triage every week, just with different words. When an incident comes in,
you don't treat every P1 the same as every P3 — you weigh how likely it is to recur against how
bad it would be if it did, and that weighing decides whether it goes to the CAB (change advisory
board) as an emergency or waits for next week's batch. Problem management runs the same motion
in reverse: find the root cause, then ask what would actually stop it from happening again versus
what would just help you notice faster next time.

The blood industry runs the identical logic, formalized under a name you'll now start seeing
constantly: **the ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management approach.** ICH stands for the International
Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use — a body
that writes harmonized guidelines adopted across pharma and biologics regulators worldwide,
including FDA. ICH Q9 is a *guideline*, not an FDA regulation and not an AABB Standard — a fourth
flavor of "you have to," issued by an international harmonization body rather than FDA. Its core
idea is the same one behind an engineering FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) risk priority
number, just applied to quality decisions instead of hardware failure modes: **rank risk by how
likely it is, how bad it would be, and how easily you'd catch it before it does damage.**

Here's the direct translation into vocabulary you already own:

- **Risk ranking (likelihood × severity × detectability)** is the same motion as scoring an
  incident or change by probability and business impact before deciding how it gets handled.
- **Preventive / detective / corrective controls** map onto problem management's "eliminate the
  root cause versus just alarm on it faster" distinction, and onto change management's choice
  between blocking a risky change outright versus having a fast, tested rollback ready.
- **Inherent vs. residual risk** is the same question you ask about any control you're about to
  invest in: how much risk is actually left over *after* you deploy it, not how much risk existed
  before you started, and not how much risk you'd like to believe is gone because a control
  exists on paper.

The value-add here isn't the concept of risk itself — you already run risk-based decisions daily.
It's this specific vocabulary, because every deviation form, CAPA template, and validation
protocol you'll review at Lakeshore assumes you already speak it fluently, the same way an ITIL
practitioner assumes everyone in the room already knows what "impact and urgency" mean.

## The vocabulary, in plain English

**Likelihood** — how probable is it that this failure mode happens (again, or at all)? For
Deviation A, the callback process failing is somewhat plausible under staffing pressure —
moderate likelihood. For Deviation B, a label swap during manual processing is a known failure
mode in any manual labeling step — also plausible, arguably higher, because it happens at a point
in the process with less redundancy built in.

**Severity** — if the failure isn't caught, how bad is the outcome? A late callback, worst case,
delays a donor's status update — annoying, low patient-safety consequence. A label swap that
reaches a hospital, worst case, means a patient receives blood typed and tracked under the wrong
donor identity — a severe patient-safety and traceability failure. Severity is where Deviation B
clearly outranks Deviation A.

**Detectability** — how likely is a failure to be caught *before* it causes harm, given the
controls already in place? This is the piece most people skip, and it's why "it didn't reach the
patient" isn't the whole story. The label mix-up was almost undetected — it survived processing
and was only caught at the very last scan, the last line of defense. The late callback was
inherently low-risk to detect, because the unit was quarantined the entire time by a separate,
independent control (quarantine status), not because anyone caught a mistake in progress. Low
detectability (hard to catch) pushes risk *up*; a near-miss caught only at the last possible
checkpoint is a flashing signal that your detection margin is thin, even though nothing bad
happened this time.

**Inherent risk vs. residual risk** — inherent risk is how risky the activity is with *no*
controls at all: manually processing and labeling two visually similar platelet units next to
each other, unaided, is inherently high-risk. Residual risk is what's left *after* your actual
controls are applied — the barcode scan, the second-check step, the quarantine hold. The label
mix-up shows why this distinction matters: residual risk looked acceptable on paper, right up
until the near-miss proved the margin between "caught" and "shipped" was one scan wide. A
control existing is not the same as residual risk being low; ask how much inherent risk the
control actually removes, and how much margin is left if it fails once.

**Preventive control** — stops the failure from happening at all. Requiring two people to
independently verify donor ID before a label prints, instead of one person doing it alone, is
preventive: it removes the opportunity for the error, not just catches it after.

**Detective control** — catches the failure after it occurs, before it causes harm. The final
barcode scan that caught the label mix-up is a detective control — it worked, but only because it
existed at the very end of the line, with nothing after it.

**Corrective control** (the "action" in CAPA) — what you do *after* a failure is caught: fix the
immediate instance, and fix the process so the same failure mode is less likely to recur. Pulling
the mislabeled unit and relabeling it correctly is a correction; redesigning the processing
station layout so visually similar units aren't placed adjacent to each other during manual
labeling is the corrective *action* — the part meant to change the future likelihood, which is
exactly problem management's "prevent recurrence" motion, just under a different name.

Notice the trap in your QA's proposed ranking: she called the label mix-up "high" (right, on
severity and thin detectability) and the callback "low" (defensible, on severity) — but "low"
doesn't mean "no CAPA." It means the corrective action might be lighter, not that closing it
with a note is correct without that same risk reasoning written down.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(c) | "Title 21, Part 606, Section 100, paragraph c" | A thorough investigation — including conclusions and followup — of any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a lot or unit to meet specifications, made and recorded. | The regulatory floor under *both* deviations: neither can be closed with a shrug, regardless of how "low" its risk ranking turns out to be. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(b)(1)(i)–(ii) | "Title 21, Part 606, Section 171, paragraph b, subparagraph 1, clauses i and ii" | Defines what makes a deviation reportable to FDA as a BPDR (biological product deviation report): a deviation from CGMP/applicable requirements, or an unexpected/unforeseeable event, that *may affect* the safety, purity, or potency of a distributed product. | The test for whether Deviation B's near-miss crosses into mandatory-reporting territory — and the reason "it didn't reach the patient" doesn't end the analysis. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(c) | "Title 21, Part 606, Section 171, paragraph c" | A 45-calendar-day reporting deadline, starting from when you acquire information reasonably suggesting a reportable event occurred — not from when the investigation finishes. | Whichever way the risk ranking lands, the reporting clock (if it applies) starts at discovery, so the ranking decision itself can't be allowed to stall. |

## The actual text

21 CFR 606.100(c) is the same "thorough investigation" language from the previous foundation
lesson, and it applies here without any carve-out for how minor a deviation looks. Quoting
verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md`:

> All records pertinent to the lot or unit maintained pursuant to these regulations shall be
> reviewed before the release or distribution of a lot or unit of final product. The review or
> portions of the review may be performed at appropriate periods during or after blood
> collecting, processing, compatibility testing and storing. A thorough investigation, including
> the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained discrepancy or the failure of a lot or unit to
> meet any of its specifications shall be made and recorded.

Read that against the risk vocabulary: "thorough investigation... conclusions and followup" is
the regulation's way of demanding you actually *do* the likelihood/severity/detectability
reasoning and write it down — not just record that something happened. A discrepancy with a
one-line closure note and no stated reasoning fails this regulation regardless of how the
deviation was ranked, because the investigation itself is the requirement, not the outcome.

Whether Deviation B has to go further — to FDA, not just into Lakeshore's own quality
record — is a separate question, answered by 606.171. Quoting verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.171.md`:

> (b) *What do I report under this section?* You must report any event, and information relevant
> to the event, associated with the manufacturing, to include testing, processing, packing,
> labeling, or storage, or with the holding or distribution, of both licensed and unlicensed
> blood or blood components, including Source Plasma, if that event meets all the following
> criteria:
>
> (1) Either:
>
> (i) Represents a deviation from current good manufacturing practice, applicable regulations,
> applicable standards, or established specifications that may affect the safety, purity, or
> potency of that product; or
>
> (ii) Represents an unexpected or unforeseeable event that may affect the safety, purity, or
> potency of that product...

Notice the word doing all the work: **"may affect."** Not "did affect." The label mix-up never
reached a patient, but a mislabeled unit — wrong donor ID on a bag that nearly shipped — is
exactly the kind of event that *may affect* traceability and, through it, safety, which is why
severity and detectability (not just "did harm occur") drive whether this section is even in
play. And critically, 606.171 only governs *distributed* product:

> (3) Involves distributed blood or blood components.

The unit in Deviation B was caught before distribution — so on the facts given, 606.171's
reporting trigger likely isn't met *for this specific unit*. But that determination itself has to
be made and documented, not assumed, because if the same failure mode had been one scan later,
the calculus flips entirely. If it does apply, the clock is unforgiving:

> (c) *When do I report under this section?* You should report a biological product deviation as
> soon as possible but you must report at a date not to exceed 45-calendar days from the date you,
> your agent, or another person who performs a manufacturing, holding, or distribution step under
> your control, acquire information reasonably suggesting that a reportable event has occurred.

That 45-day clock starts on *discovery*, before the investigation is even finished. This is why
risk ranking can't be a leisurely exercise — the reportability question has to be asked early,
even if the final answer is "no."

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reviewing this month's deviation log doesn't just check
whether Deviation B got a CAPA and Deviation A didn't. They look for a **documented risk
assessment or justification** attached to each deviation, showing the actual reasoning: what was
the likelihood, what was the severity, what was the detectability, and did the response actually
match that reasoning. "Closed — no patient impact" is not that document. It states an outcome,
not a rationale, and it's the single most common gap investigators find in deviation files —
not that the wrong decision was made, but that no one can show *how* the decision was made.

For Deviation B specifically, they'll also want the 606.171 reportability determination in
writing — even if the conclusion is "not reportable, distribution never occurred" — because a
near-miss with no documented reportability analysis reads as an oversight or an avoided question.
The document that protects Lakeshore isn't the CAPA alone; it's the risk reasoning behind it,
owned by Quality, expected to exist *before* anyone asks for it.

## Common traps

**"Severity is the only thing that matters — rank by worst-case outcome and stop there."** This
is the trap in treating "no patient impact" as the end of the analysis. Two deviations with
identical worst-case severity can carry very different real risk once you factor in likelihood
and detectability. A label mix-up caught only at the last possible scan has a thinner safety
margin than one caught three checkpoints earlier — same severity, very different residual risk.

**"A control exists on paper, so residual risk is low."** The barcode scan existed the whole
time Deviation B was in process — it just happened to be the *last* line of defense, not one of
several. A control's existence tells you nothing about how much inherent risk it actually
removes, or how much margin is left if it's the only thing standing between a mistake and a
shipped unit. Assess residual risk against what the control catches and where it sits in the
process, not against whether a line for it exists in the SOP.

**"The barcode scan that caught the mix-up is a corrective action — problem solved."** It's not.
The scan is a *detective* control — it caught the error after it happened, which is valuable,
but it did nothing to stop the mislabeling and doesn't reduce the likelihood of the next one.
Confusing "we caught it" (detective) with "we fixed it" (corrective) is how a CAPA gets closed
after adding zero preventive value — the process that produced the error stays untouched.

## What this means for your job

- **When a QA hands you a risk ranking, ask for all three factors, not just severity.** If the
  write-up only answers "how bad," send it back before it reaches the quality council.
- **Treat a near-miss caught at the last checkpoint as a real signal, not a save.** "It didn't
  reach the patient" isn't "the risk was low." Ask what would have happened if the control that
  caught it had run a half-second later, or hadn't run at all.
- **When someone proposes a fix, ask which control type it actually is before you approve it.**
  "We'll watch for it more closely" is detective, not preventive. If every CAPA response in a
  file is detective-only, that pattern is worth escalating on its own.
- **Ask explicitly whether a deviation's 606.171 reportability has been assessed and documented,
  every time — even when the answer is "no."** The absence of that determination is itself the
  finding an inspector will flag, regardless of whether reporting was actually required.
- **"Closed, no patient impact" is a conclusion with the reasoning missing, not a risk
  assessment.** If that's the entire justification on file, 606.100(c)'s investigation
  requirement isn't satisfied yet, no matter how the ranking would have come out on paper.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says the likelihood × severity × detectability risk-ranking method is "an FDA requirement for every deviation." Accurate?

Not quite. The three-factor risk-ranking approach comes from the ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management
guideline — an international harmonization guideline, not an FDA regulation, and not something
21 CFR 606 spells out by name or by formula. What *is* an FDA regulatory requirement is 606.100(c):
a thorough, documented investigation of any discrepancy. ICH Q9's likelihood/severity/detectability
structure is simply the accepted, defensible *method* the industry uses to make that investigation
rigorous rather than arbitrary — it's guidance-tier methodology in service of a regulation-tier
requirement, not itself codified law. Calling it "the regulation" is the same category mistake the
previous foundation lesson covered, just with a different source at the top of the pyramid.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The label mix-up (Deviation B) never reached a patient. Does that mean it doesn't need a 606.171 reportability review at all?

No — and this is the trap in the scenario. 606.171's trigger language is "may affect" safety,
purity, or potency, not "did affect," and it explicitly covers events that are unexpected or
unforeseeable even without confirmed harm. What *does* matter for 606.171 specifically is
paragraph (b)(3): the event has to involve *distributed* product. Since this unit was caught
before it left the building, the reporting trigger likely isn't met on these facts — but "likely
isn't met" still has to be a documented determination, made and filed, not an assumption skipped
because nothing bad happened. Skipping the documentation is the finding, even when the eventual
conclusion turns out to be correct.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The barcode scan caught the mislabeled unit before it shipped. Your QA calls the scan itself "the corrective action" and wants to close the deviation on that basis. Correct?

No. The scan is a detective control — it caught an error that had already occurred, which is
exactly its job, but it didn't prevent the mislabeling and it doesn't reduce the likelihood of it
happening again. A corrective action has to address the failure mode itself: relabeling the
specific unit correctly is the immediate correction, and something like changing how similar
units are physically separated during manual labeling, or requiring independent verification
before a label prints, would be the corrective *action* that actually lowers future likelihood.
Calling the detective control "the fix" and closing the deviation there leaves the root cause
completely untouched.
:::

## Where this goes next

That's the third and final foundation module. Between this lesson and `regulatory-landscape-
orientation`, you can now do two things every downstream course assumes: sort any rule into
statute, regulation, guidance, or standard and say which one binds — and rank any deviation,
vendor gap, or system finding by likelihood, severity, and detectability, then say plainly
whether a proposed fix is preventive, detective, or corrective. The curriculum now moves into
Track 1, `blood-center-operations`, where you'll walk the actual donor-to-hospital pipeline and
start placing both of these vocabularies against real regulated steps — not hypothetical
deviations, but the specific points in the process where a likelihood-severity-detectability
call and a regulation-versus-guidance call both have to happen in real time.
